title: Stories and Prayers of St. Nicholas
subtitle: A retelling of the Three Bags of Gold and the troparion of his feast
source: The Three Bags of Gold is an editorial retelling of the story preserved in the Synaxaria of the fourth through ninth centuries. The troparion (apolytikion) of the December 6 feast is in the public-domain English of The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom: The Greek Text with a Rendering in English (London: Williams & Norgate, 1914), and the opening of the kontakion, in a note, in that of Isabel Florence Hapgood, Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic (Greco-Russian) Church (Boston, 1906).

sections.title: The three bags of gold
sections.framing: The story of the three bags of gold is preserved in the Synaxaria of the fourth through ninth centuries, the short lives of saints read at Matins. Distilled into folklore over a thousand years, it is the seed of every later legend of gifts that arrive at night in winter. The Orthodox memory keeps the original sharper: this was almsgiving against the trafficking of three poor sisters, given by a priest who refused to be thanked. The paragraphs below are a narrative retelling of the Synaxarion, not a direct quotation.
paragraphs: In the town of Patara, while Nicholas was still a young deacon, lived a man who had once been rich and was now ruined. He had three daughters and no dowry for any of them. Their marriages were impossible, and he was preparing to sell them into shame in order to feed them.

Nicholas heard of it. He took a leather purse, filled it with the gold his parents had left him, and that night dropped it in secret through a window of the man's house. The eldest was married the next month. The middle daughter's turn came; again at night a second purse arrived through the window. By the third night the father was watching, and when Nicholas threw the third purse and turned to run, the man chased him into the street and caught him by the cloak.

He fell at the deacon's feet, weeping, and called him father, saviour, and friend. Nicholas told him to say nothing of it while he lived. The Synaxarion has not kept the man's name. It has kept what Nicholas did: three poor daughters spared the wages of poverty by a gift no one asked them to repay.
notes: Patara is on the southern coast of modern Turkey. The ruins of its harbour and basilica can still be visited.

The story of the bags of gold is the historical bedrock under every later Nicholas legend, the bishop in red, the gifts in the stockings, the December night. The Orthodox memory keeps the original meaning: alms given in secret, against trafficking, refused thanks.

sections.title: Troparion of St. Nicholas
sections.framing: The troparion is the standard hymn for any saint commemorated at Liturgy. Each saint has his own; their texts are among the densest theology the Church sings. The phrase 'rule of faith' (kanon pisteos) was used by Irenaeus and the early Fathers for the apostolic confession against the Gnostics, applying it to a bishop of the third century is no small praise. The hymn does not mention the wonders, the storms calmed, the prisoners delivered, the dead raised. In the Greek it says only: rule of faith, image of meekness, teacher of self-control. The wonders rest on the man. The man rests on Christ.
sections.citation: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Greek and English (London, 1914), pp. 124-125, the Dismissal Hymn for December 6
paragraphs: The Truth of thy deeds has shown thee to thy flock as a Canon of the Faith, an example of Virtue, and a teacher of Abstinence;
wherefore thou didst by humility acquire greatness, and by poverty, riches.
O Father and Saint, Nicholas, intercede with Christ our God, that our souls may be saved.
notes: Sung at every Liturgy of St. Nicholas in every Orthodox church on the sixth of December, and at Vespers of his feast the night before.

The Orthodox tradition pairs the troparion with the kontakion, a longer hymn that names the specifics of the saint's life. The kontakion of St. Nicholas opens, in Hapgood's English (1906, p. 61): 'In Myra, O Saint, wast thou shown forth a sacrificing priest...'
